senses.definition: To build a skill through repeated practice instead of one-off training.
senses.caution: It says the ability is missing today. Said about another team that is a criticism in gym clothes; said about your own it is an admission, which is fine only if the next sentence names the actual reps. To a team already at capacity it lands as more work with no more people. It is also coaching-deck language, so in a written board paper it reads as a slogan and invites the obvious question of what the exercise is and who is doing it.
senses.example: We can buy the first three evaluations in. If we want this capability in-house, at some point we have to build that muscle ourselves.

cues.text: Your team keeps handing evaluation work to a consultancy, and you want to argue for doing it in-house repeatedly until they are good at it.
A director asks why you are giving juniors the client presentations when a senior would do a better job today, and your answer is about where the team is in a year.
A friend says they are simply hopeless at cooking, and you want to say the ability is not fixed and comes from doing it over and over.
You have started running twice a week and are explaining to a sceptical relative why the first month feeling awful is the whole point.

distractors: To use your own product for real work before asking anyone else to.
To make a bad situation worse than it already was.
To dig patiently through records for something that was never hidden on purpose.
To replace a running part of a system without stopping the system around it.
To put right something that was wrong.
